title: Emperor Taizong Lets the Condemned Go Home
text:
In the year 632 Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty, reviewing the cases of prisoners condemned to death, was moved by pity. According to the Chinese histories, he ordered that 390 of them be sent home to their families. They were to return to the capital on a set day the following autumn to be executed.

No guards went with them. When the appointed day came in 633, every one of the 390 returned of their own accord to face death. The emperor was so impressed that he pardoned them all.

The story was retold for centuries as proof of how a ruler's virtue could transform even criminals. In the 11th century the Song statesman and historian Ouyang Xiu wrote a famous essay, On Releasing Prisoners, questioning it. He argued that the emperor released them expecting them to return so he could pardon them, and the prisoners returned expecting to be pardoned, so each side was performing for the other. Good rule, he said, depended on steady laws, not on gestures that could not be repeated.
lesson: Trust given openly can call out trustworthiness in others. But ask whether a gesture builds a lasting system or only a good story.
people: Emperor Taizong of Tang, Ouyang Xiu
source: Sima Guang, Zizhi Tongjian, chapter 194; Ouyang Xiu, "On Releasing Prisoners" (Zong Qiu Lun)
caveat: Ouyang Xiu and later critics suspected the episode was staged for political effect.
